timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Hey guys, welcome back.
So I've been seeing a lot of posts on the forums lately from new equinox owners who were
complaining that they'll get a good signal but once they dig into the ground, it either
disappears or it turns out to be a bent nail or some other piece of iron junk. That's what
you call a falseing and today I'm going to try to find an example of that and show it
alongside of a good target and hopefully explain the difference between the two and maybe
help some people cut down on the amount of junk targets they're digging. So stick around
and we'll get started.
Okay, here we have what I believe is going to be a good example of falseing. And one thing
you'll notice right away is that the signal seems to be hit or miss and the numbers are
kind of all over the place. When you get on a good target, that tone is going to be there
every single time so long as you keep your swing speed consistent and your call location
the same. This one not so much. Another dead giveaway to falseing iron is a lot of times
when you go to pinpoint the pinpoint location. It'll be off by a couple of inches compared
to where you originally heard the tone.
All right, let's dig this one up and verify that it is indeed falseing iron.
There you go, the rusty nail.
Even more in the hole.
Okay, here I have what I think is going to be a good target. As long as I keep my swing speed
and my call location in the same spot, the tone is there every single time.
I do is stay in in the mid-20s for the most part. All right, let's dig it up and see what it is.
That's going to be a penny. Until if that's a weedy or a couple of memorial.
There you have it guys, hopefully that's useful to at least a few people. Now I'm no Equinox
or anything like that. This is just what works best for me. I do realize there's some other methods for checking falseing
but I feel like most of those have some drawbacks. For example, you can always bump up your iron bias.
But if you do that it's a trade-off. You're going to give up some separation.
And then some people like to listen for the iron buzz on the edge of the call. But I've found that you've got to be careful with the deeper targets
because the deeper it is the more the ground starts to consume the target. And you'll get some iron buzz even on good metals.
And then you can always switch frequencies and check the target again. But the last thing I really want to do on the field
is have to do a bunch of button presses. I'd rather just train my ear that way. I know instantly whether I have a good target or not.
But anyway, that's it for now. Thanks for watching. Happy hunting. And I'll see you next time.

youtube_description:
Here I show a falsing signal and compare it to an obvious good signal, in hopes of helping frustrated new Equinox users cut down on the amount of junk targets they dig while getting used to the machine. On good targets co-located with iron it can be a little more tricky, so the old saying still holds true.. When in doubt, dig it out.
